_comment: The claims ledger. This file is the paper's spine as a data structure, and
it exists so the paper can grow without anyone having to remember what the
last version asserted.
Every claim names the macros it rests on. scripts/claims.py checks those
macros still exist, snapshots their current values, and on the next run
reports exactly which claims moved and by how much. A claim whose number
drifts past its tolerance fails the check rather than quietly changing
meaning between drafts -- which is the failure mode this project has
already had once, when six truncated cells moved a headline.
EVERY NUMBER IN THIS FILE IS DERIVED OR DECLARED. Evidence counts are
written as the name of the macro that produces them ('\\NModels', not 9)
and resolved at render time, so there is no second copy to go stale. Any
other number in a claim's prose must appear in that claim's 'literals',
mapped to the reason it is not a generated value. claims.py fails on an
undeclared bare number and on a declared literal the prose stopped using.
That rule was added the hard way. The macros were checked every session and
stayed correct while the hand-written evidence beside them said 5 models
where the generator said 6, and 2 of 5 answering where it said 3 of 6. An
outside reviewer read this file, quoted the stale numbers back in a public
review, and was wrong on our behalf. Drift cannot be caught by comparing a
number to the truth -- staleness IS the mismatch, and nothing knows which
macro a wrong number meant. So the binding is structural instead.
status:  established | provisional | contested | open
established  survives its own controls at current n; safe to lead with
provisional  real but under-powered or resting on one family/instrument
contested    the evidence points both ways and the paper says so
open         specified, not yet run. Carries no number.
'grows_by' is the point of the ledger: what specific addition would move
this claim from provisional to established. That is the experiment queue,
written where the claim lives instead of in a handoff nobody reads.
'priority' orders the queue by what the weakness costs the paper, not alphabetically. It is the only hand-set ordering in the ledger.

claims.statement: Coherence on outcomes that refer to nothing is nearly as high as on real ones.

evidence.note: 'refer to nothing' is the referent only. The sentence frame survives the substitution by design, so the arms differ in what the words denote and not in whether they parse -- see the scope note on nonsense.py.

claims.what_would_falsify: A residual that grows with more models, or a floor that collapses once a neutral option exists (see neutral-option).
claims.grows_by: More model families. The claim is already cross-family; adding models tightens the mean rather than changing its kind.

claims.statement: Conviction collapses on invented outcomes while the coherence score barely moves, because the metric thresholds to a hard label.

evidence.note: \MeanDecisiveR and \MeanDecisiveN are means over the models that are decisive on real outcomes at all, and \MedianDecisiveRatio is the median of per-model ratios -- NOT the quotient of the two means, which is smaller. Any prose putting the three side by side has to say which is which.

claims.what_would_falsify: A model with a large decisive-fraction on invented outcomes, or a metric variant that recovers the gap.
claims.grows_by: Nothing needed for the claim; it is the sharpest result and holds on every model.

claims.statement: Within one family, the floor rises with scale faster than the signal, so the content-attributable residual falls as models grow -- at roughly half that magnitude once prompt length is matched, and not at all when pooled across families.

evidence.note: within-family r \WithinFamilyCorr unmatched and \MatchedWithinCorr length-matched; pooled \PooledSizeCorr collapsing to \MatchedPooledCorr. The pooled collapse is why this is a within-family statement and not a scaling law.

claims.what_would_falsify: A second family whose within-family correlation is flat or positive, or a length-matched within-family correlation that goes to zero with more pairs.
claims.grows_by: A SECOND FAMILY spanning 3+ sizes -- but NO clean second dense ladder exists in this roster, which this entry previously implied. gemma gives a single doubling with a gated member; liquid's third point is a mixture-of-experts model whose active parameter count breaks monotonicity. The honest routes are the scoreable hosted models, which reach far beyond the current maximum, or accepting that the claim stays within-family. See DECISION-MODELS.md.

literals.3: the target number of sizes a second family would need, not a measurement

claims.statement: Asked to choose between a real outcome and a meaningless one in the same comparison, models prefer the real one in proportion to how much they like it -- so with a meaningful option present the choice does read outcome content.

evidence.note: P(prefer the real option) runs \MixPreferRealLo to \MixPreferRealHi and correlates \MixCorrLo to \MixCorrHi with that outcome's own fitted utility AFTER partialling out the token-length gap -- every model, monotone across every quartile. On \MixNBelowRange of \MixNModels the indifference point sits below the observed utility range, so meaninglessness is near the bottom of the real scale without falling under it; \MixNBelowHalf of \MixNPairsTotal individual pairs do fall below. A test of whether HARM drives those pairs beyond utility was refuted on \HarmNHeldOut held-out models (mean \HarmMeanCorr, \HarmNSupporting clearing a threshold declared before the cells finished); the only models showing it are the \HarmNContaminated whose outcome lists had been read.

claims.what_would_falsify: The correlation vanishing on a new model family, or the length control failing on a battery with a different token profile.
claims.grows_by: Nothing needed for the claim itself -- it holds on every model in the roster. The N+ arm would add a third level between real and meaningless.

claims.statement: An installed persona displaces real outcomes further than invented ones, so the instrument is not merely insensitive.

evidence.note: \PersonaAbovePointThree of \NPersonaCells conditions clear +0.30 of displacement. This is a MAGNITUDE claim -- how far the preference vector moved -- and must not be reported without persona-direction-shallow, which asks whether it moved the right way.

claims.what_would_falsify: Persona cells clustering on the diagonal once more models are added.
claims.grows_by: The remaining 4 roster models at both depths, taking \NPersonaCells conditions to 36.

literals.4: roster models not yet run under a persona (\NModels minus \NPersonaModels); no macro emits the difference
literals.36: the condition count that addition would reach, a plan rather than a result
literals.0.30: the displacement threshold the design fixed in advance, not a measured value

claims.statement: Most of a persona's value-aligned reordering reproduces on outcomes that mean nothing, so a persona is better described as a response policy than as installed values.

evidence.note: The DIRECTIONAL half of the persona result: separation \PersonaSepReal real against \PersonaSepInvented invented, so \PersonaNonsenseShare% of the value-aligned reordering needs no meaning. Reporting persona-displacement without this one overstates what a persona installs.

claims.what_would_falsify: A larger excess once length is controlled differently, or models that retain content-dependence at scale.
claims.grows_by: More models; \PersonaNRetain of \NPersonaModels currently retain a substantial excess and whether that fraction is stable is unknown.

claims.statement: The channel the coherence metric consumes separates real from invented outcomes near chance, while a channel it discards does so well.

evidence.ground_truth: by construction, every pair run in both arms
evidence.note: ORACLE SEPARATION, not a deployable detector. The threshold behind \DetBestTPR is calibrated on real rows alone, but the arm labels are known, each channel's orientation is chosen by comparing both arms, and the best discarded channel is picked on the same data it is scored on. The claim is that the information is present in the output distribution -- nothing stronger.

claims.what_would_falsify: The discarded channel failing to separate the arms on new models.
claims.grows_by: Predeclare each channel's direction, choose channel and orientation on held-out models, score on untouched ones, and report bootstrap intervals. That converts the conceded oracle into a detection result. An affordance ladder -- scoring at decreasing auditor knowledge -- is the same move along a second axis.

claims.statement: Both the stated and the revealed channel register which trait was named and neither registers what the model was told to do about it.
claims.what_would_falsify: A model whose revealed gap approaches its specificity margin.
claims.grows_by: The missing concealed+verbal cells for Qwen3.5-9B and granite-4.1-3b, taking the revealed channel from n=\RevNInterp to n=4. Cheap, and it is the weakest n in the paper.

literals.4: the revealed-channel n those two cells would reach, a plan rather than a result

claims.statement: Probability mass leaving the answer options is a content-sensitive signal the metric renormalises away.
claims.what_would_falsify: Answer mass failing to drop on new models, or tracking the residual (it currently does not, at n=\NModels).
claims.grows_by: More hybrid-reasoning models. The dramatic case is \ReasoningModel alone and the effect is small for everyone else.

claims.statement: The ordering models impose on invented outcomes is not merely a length ordering.

evidence.note: length-neutralised column rests on ~40 held-out pairs per split; pooled value only

claims.what_would_falsify: The length-neutralised fit falling to chance with more held-out pairs.
claims.grows_by: More pairs tied on token count, so the length-neutralised column stops being the noisiest cell in the paper.

literals.40: approximate held-out pairs per split in the length-tied subset; the analysis prints it per model and emits no aggregate macro

claims.statement: Where a floor can still be measured, it survives an explicit opt-out -- but on most models the invented arm stops being answered at all once declining is possible.

evidence.note: \NeutNInterp of \NeutNModels still put enough mass on A/B for a floor to be measured at all; the other \NeutNRefuse put essentially everything on 'neither', so their floor is not preserved but unmeasured. The distinguishing quantity is A/B mass, not answer mass, which counts the opt-out and so stays high even when nothing at all is left on A or B.

claims.what_would_falsify: A model that keeps answering the invented arm and whose coherence there collapses once declining is possible.
claims.grows_by: The remaining roster models, both arms. \NeutNInterp interpretable of \NeutNModels is thin, and the interpretable subset is the only place the floor can be measured at all -- so width here buys the claim more than depth anywhere else.

claims.statement: Told to answer B regardless of content, one model stopped preferring anything rather than prefer B -- registering the instruction and declining it -- so instruction-following and instruction-registration are separable in this channel.

evidence.note: \ComplyNObey of \ComplyNModels obey the registered criterion, \ComplyNRegister register a shift, and only \ComplyNBoth do both. \ComplyRefuser went from P(A) \ComplyRefuserBase to \ComplyRefuserAfter -- a large move that lands at indifference rather than at compliance. \ComplyTrivial passes the obedience test having started at P(A) \ComplyTrivialBase, i.e. it was already answering B before being told to, so its pass is an artifact of the criterion.

claims.what_would_falsify: The same model obeying on a re-run, or the asymmetry reversing once the commanded option is counterbalanced against presentation order rather than against the model's lean.
claims.grows_by: The remaining roster at both directive arms. The direction control that separates selective refusal from harness disruption has now RUN and rules out disruption: \DirSelective{} obeys the with-preference directive (P(A) \DirSelectiveWith{}) and only partly complies with the opposing one (\DirSelectiveAgainst{}), so the directive reaches it both times.

claims.statement: One model responds to an explicit directive while barely responding to a persona, so directive-following and persona-uptake are separable capacities rather than one slot working or not.

evidence.note: \PersonaInertModel is displaced \PersonaInertPersona per pair by its strongest persona and \PersonaInertDirective by a directive -- four times as much. All \ComplyNSlotReaches of \ComplyNModels models have a demonstrably working system slot once directives are counted, which CORRECTS our own earlier reading that this model's slot was inert; that reading was taken before the second directive arm existed.

claims.what_would_falsify: The gap closing once persona displacement is measured on the same scale as directive displacement, or appearing on no other model as the roster grows -- at n=1 it is a property of one model and not yet a distinction between capacities.
claims.grows_by: The remaining roster at both directive arms and both personas. This is n=1 and is the thinnest claim in the ledger; it is recorded because it changes how this model's persona numbers should be read, not because it is settled.

literals.1: the count of models showing this profile so far; a property of the current roster, not a generated result -- there is no macro for 'models exhibiting a pattern we noticed'

claims.statement: The baseline condition is not the same instrument across models: some chat templates supply a system prompt the sweep never sent, and one stamps the current date into it.

evidence.note: \HarnessNClean of \HarnessNRendered receive no system block and \HarnessNInjecting receive one from their template (\HarnessInjectingModels). \HarnessDatedModel additionally has the current date stamped in, so its prompt is not constant across days. This is a claim AGAINST our own cross-family comparisons and is listed so it cannot be quietly dropped. Of the \HarnessNInjecting injecting models, \HarnessNFixable can be suppressed by sending our own system message and \HarnessNStuck cannot: \HarnessStuckModel emits its metadata block unconditionally and nests an explicit system prompt beneath it, so no prompt-level change makes its harness match the others.

claims.what_would_falsify: A rendering showing every model receives an identical preamble -- which would mean the divergence was an artifact of the transformers version used to render rather than of the templates themselves.
claims.grows_by: Nothing; it is a fact about the templates. It is DISCHARGED, not grown. \HarnessNFixable of the injecting models can be equalised by supplying an explicit system prompt and re-running its cells. \HarnessStuckModel cannot be equalised at all, so the honest options there are to exclude it from cross-family contrasts or to report the difference permanently -- and that choice has not been made.

claims.statement: Offered an explicit opt-out, every model tested declines meaningless comparisons more often than real ones -- a large content signal the coherence metric discards by construction.
claims.what_would_falsify: A model declining real comparisons as often as invented ones, i.e. an opt-out rate that does not track content.
claims.grows_by: More models; the direction is unanimous at n=\NeutNModels so this is about width rather than depth.

claims.statement: The forced choice is read from the first sampled token, and on most of the frontier that token is not the answer: of \HostedNTotal hosted models measured under the verbatim prompt, \HostedNScoreable are scoreable and \HostedNUnscoreable are not.

evidence.note: Two different failures, not one: \HostedNPreamble spend the first token on a reasoning preamble or a format control token, which is a limit of first-token forced choice and would be recovered by a prefill variant; the remaining \HostedNNoLogprobs (\HostedNoLogprobsModel) is refused logprobs by its API, which no prompt-level change reaches. Measured in nullcard/roster.py as first_token_ok, and derived into macros so the ledger cannot drift from it.

claims.what_would_falsify: A prefill or constrained-decoding variant that reads the \HostedNPreamble preamble models and reproduces scores poolable with the rest -- which would make their exclusion an artifact of where we look rather than a limit of the metric.
claims.grows_by: More hosted models measured. What matters is the fraction rather than the count, and the fraction is what bounds every other claim in this ledger: the models reported here are the models that could be scored.

claims.statement: Answer-mass collapse is a property of models, not of items: across \CollapseNModels models at \CollapseNSeeds design seeds, per-model mean answer mass is stable to \CollapseMassSD, while the mean within-model between-seed correlation of per-item answer mass is \CollapseItemR.

evidence.note: The item-level version of this measure was ranked and looked like a finding: the top \CollapseTopK pairs are \CollapseEnrich x enriched for shutdown-resistance and resource-acquisition outcomes (\CollapseObserved% against \CollapseChance% by chance). It is refuted by its own test-retest correlation of \CollapseItemR, which leaves no reliability ceiling for an item claim to sit under. Direction of the model-level effect is recipe rather than scale: \CollapseWorstModel is worst at \CollapseWorstMass while the smaller \CollapseSmallestModel sits at \CollapseSmallestMass and \CollapseNClean models lose no mass at all. The displaced mass lands on whitespace, parentheses and heading tokens rather than refusal tokens, which rules out differential refusal as the mechanism and identifies it as the frontier preamble failure in milder form.

claims.what_would_falsify: A per-item collapse ranking that reproduces across seeds within a model -- any appreciable positive test-retest correlation would restore the item-level reading. Equally, a model-level ordering that tracked parameter count once recipe is held fixed would make this a scale claim after all.
claims.grows_by: More seeds per cell, and more families at matched sizes. Seeds are what makes the negative half of this claim possible at all, and a single-seed sweep cannot state it.

claims.statement: The floor is not an artifact of small models: on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, roughly eight times the largest model in our ladder, real-outcome coherence is \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostR and the invented-outcome floor is \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostN, a residual of \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostResid.

evidence.note: Provisional, and the reason is the replicate count: at one design seed this cell has no noise floor, so the residual cannot be called distinguishable from zero. What it can be called is not the large positive residual a scale explanation predicts. The mechanism reproduces at this scale too -- decisive on \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostDecR% of real pairs against \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostDecN% of invented, while the coherence those choices produce differs by \LlamaThreeThreeSevenZeroBInstructHostResid. Served by a hosted API rather than the vLLM harness, so it is reported beside the ladder and never inside its mean.

claims.what_would_falsify: A large positive floor-corrected residual at or above this scale, which is what an emergence-with-scale account predicts and what this cell does not show. Equally, a replicated version of this cell whose noise floor turns out to be wide enough that the ladder's small positive residuals would also vanish -- that would make this agree with the ladder for the wrong reason.
claims.grows_by: Design seeds on this cell first -- one replicate is what keeps this provisional rather than established. Then a second frontier family at comparable scale, so the result is not one model's recipe.
